item.title: Adam Carolla credits Jimmy Kimmel for comedy career, warns society collapses when comics stop telling truth
item.description: Jimmy Kimmel was the first person to tell Adam Carolla he should pursue comedy, sparking a friendship that began with early-morning boxing training at KROQ.
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Adam Carolla said Jimmy Kimmel was the first person in his life to tell him he was funny and should pursue a career in entertainment, recalling on Tuesday's episode of "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" how the encouragement grew out of an unlikely relationship that began with boxing lessons.

"He wasn't a good boxer, but he was a good comedian, and he was the first guy in my entire life to ever go, 'You are funny, man. You should be doing this,'" Carolla said.

The friendship began with Carolla finding himself locked out of KROQ radio station, where Kimmel worked at the time, at 6 a.m. Eventually, Carolla spotted someone using their keycard to enter the building, and he asked the man to relay the message that there was a boxing trainer waiting outside.

JEFF FOXWORTHY PULLS BACK THE CURTAIN ON COMEDY'S CREATIVE PROCESS FOR WHAT COULD BE HIS LAST SPECIAL

Twenty minutes later, Kimmel — who at that time was known as Jimmy the Sports Guy for the radio segment he hosted — let him into the building to begin their training.

"I ended up talking to him more about comedy than I did about boxing," said Carolla.

Carolla also touched on the importance of comedians speaking truth to power during the podcast, warning that society is in trouble when comics stop being able to joke honestly.

CONAN O'BRIEN, ZACH GALIFIANAKIS SAY IT'S A 'MISCONCEPTION' THAT COMEDY SHOWS ONLY TARGET CONSERVATIVES

"I think comedians need to sort of be truth tellers," he said, adding that during the coronavirus pandemic, "they got to the comedians."

During the pandemic, the comedian commented on facing calls to be canceled over jokes, criticism, and creative content. He has referred to those privy to cancel culture in both Hollywood and government alike as "cowards."

"Once they get to the comedians, we're in trouble," he warned Hannity on Tuesday. 

"Because you can get to the union guys because they're worried about their job, and you can get to the school teachers, and you can get to the politicians. You can get to about everybody because their job is to not get fired. But when you get to the comedians, that's a bad sign for society. And I was saddened to see that they had gotten to some of the comedians."

item.title: Rory McIlroy not bothered by Trump's expected appearance at Irish Open: 'Who are we to say no?'
item.description: Rory McIlroy downplayed distractions from Trump's expected visit to Doonbeg, calling the Irish Open host course an "Americanised" links layout.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump is expected to make an appearance during the latter stages of this week's Irish Open, and while defending champion Rory McIlroy admitted it will make things a bit "different," he's not giving too much thought to the potential distraction.

Trump is set for a two-day trip to Ireland this upcoming weekend, and with the Irish Open being played at his resort in the County Clare village of Doonbeg, his making a quick stop and potentially handing the trophy to the champion on Sunday makes plenty of sense.

McIlroy, who has played golf with President Trump in the past, did not engage in any political chatter when asked about the U.S. President's expected arrival, but instead kept the focus on the golf and the task at hand.

"It's going to be different, but the one thing I'd say is his golf resorts have hosted PGA Tour events, European Tour events, LIV events," McIlroy told BBC Sport.

"He's a big fan of golf, he's a wonderful supporter of golf. He's got a beautiful property here in Doonbeg - it's the first time I've played it. I wouldn't say it's a true links golf course, it's a bit of an Americanised version of a links course, but it's still a great golf course and should provide a good test for the week.

"It's going to be different with him being here but we're here to play a golf tournament and it's a good golf course and keep our head down and play."

TRUMP CONGRATULATES RORY MCILROY ON BACK-TO-BACK MASTERS WINS: 'BECOMING MORE AND MORE A LEGEND'

With the name 'Trump' on the entrance of the property, the president can't exactly be told he can't attend the event and watch a bit of the action, which McIlroy is also very aware of.

"Obviously, there's a lot that goes on. So, logistically, it provides some challenges, absolutely. But at the same time, if he wants to come and watch the Irish Open, who are we to say no?"

Beyond Trump making a public appearance at one of the premier golf tournaments across the pond, this week's Irish Open could be viewed as a test run for future events, most notably The Open.

Turnberry, the well-known venue in Scotland, was part of The Open's rota of courses and played host to the major championship four times between 1977 and 2009. Trump purchased the resort in 2014, and the R&A, which organizes the championship, has not brought The Open back to the property since the acquisition, while consistently citing logistical issues as the biggest hurdle.

item.title: LEE CARTER: The summer polls missed the point: Voters are moving — and the midterms begin
item.description: Summer polls carry a giant asterisk as the real midterm electorate forms now, with grocery prices and checkout costs driving the key voter concerns.
item.content:encoded:
If you think you know who’s winning the midterms, I have some bad news.

The voters who will decide them are just starting to pay attention.

I say this as someone who loves polls. They tell us what people care about, what they’re worried about and where the political opportunities are.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: VOTERS SAY THEY’RE IN ECONOMIC PAIN, BUT WILL DEMOCRATS GAIN?

But summer horse-race numbers come with a giant asterisk:

The electorate isn’t finished yet.

We saw it all summer.

In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed appeared headed toward a comfortable Democratic Senate primary victory. He won by about a point.

LEE CARTER: ELECTION SHOCKER: THE WINNERS HAD A SLOGAN; THE LOSERS JUST HAD RÉSUMÉS

In Wisconsin, Francesca Hong led David Crowley by roughly 20 points in two polls. Crowley won.

In Minnesota, a public poll had Angie Craig ahead of Peggy Flanagan by two. Flanagan won by nearly 20.

100 DAYS UNTIL MIDTERMS AND DEMOCRATS ARE WINNING BECAUSE THEY ACTUALLY HAVE A MESSAGE

The lesson isn’t that polls are wrong.

It’s that voters move.

And now comes the part of the campaign when they start moving.

Labor Day is the unofficial beginning of the election season for the people who don’t spend August obsessing over politics.

Which is to say: most people.

They don’t know who won the week. They didn’t see the viral clip. They aren’t refreshing the generic ballot. They have never described themselves as "low-propensity voters."

They’re busy.

And politics has developed a very bad habit of confusing the people who are paying the most attention with the people who will ultimately decide the election.

CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION

We confuse loud with large.

A few thousand furious people can generate an enormous amount of internet.

Millions of people wondering why their grocery bill is still so high can generate almost none.

Then Election Day comes along and counts them exactly the same.

This is why I’m less interested in who moved from 47 to 48 this week than in what sits underneath the number.

REDISTRICTING GIVES REPUBLICANS AN EDGE, BUT AFFORDABILITY WILL DECIDE THE MIDTERMS

Who is certain?

Who is movable?

Who is going to vote?

And which party is actually reaching people who weren’t already with them?

Because there is a huge difference between making your supporters more enthusiastic and turning more people into your supporters.

Attention feels like momentum. Persuasion creates it.

Which makes what Republicans are doing in Dallas this week fascinating.

For the first time, the GOP is holding a national convention built around a midterm election.

They wanted the stage.

They got it.

Now the question is whether they use it to talk to themselves or to the voters they still need.

DAVID MARCUS: EXPERTS CROWNED EL-SAYED — THEN MICHIGAN VOTERS TURNED HIS WIN INTO A NEAR-DISASTER

Because Republicans don’t have an awareness problem.

Everyone knows Donald Trump.

They don’t have an enthusiasm problem among their most loyal supporters.

They have an affordability problem.

100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY

Americans don’t experience the economy through a press release.

They experience it at checkout.

Washington has statistics. Americans have receipts.

They know what groceries cost. They know what happened to their insurance premium. They know what the electric bill looks like. They know whether a decent salary suddenly doesn’t feel so decent anymore.

Republicans can spend their time in Dallas explaining why the economy is better.

Or they can answer the question voters are actually asking:

When does my life get more affordable?

That’s the opening.

RECORD GAS PRICES SQUEEZE AMERICANS AS SUMMER TRAVEL SEASON ENDS, MIDTERMS LOOM AND IRAN WAR WAGES ON

And Democrats see it too.

Texas Democrat James Talarico is counterprogramming the Republican convention with a statewide food drive focused on grocery prices and affordability.

It’s almost painfully perfect.

Republicans have the arena. Democrats want the grocery cart.

That’s the midterm fight.

Republicans can use Dallas to make people who already love Trump cheer louder.

Or they can give people who aren’t sold on Republicans a reason to reconsider.

One produces a great television moment.

The other produces votes.

And that’s what I’ll be watching in every poll from here to November.

Not simply who is ahead.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Who is moving?

Who is persuadable?

Who is expanding their coalition?

Who is turning concern into choice and enthusiasm into turnout?

The political class spent the summer measuring attention.

Now we get to measure something much more important.

Persuasion.

The midterms start now.

Republicans go first.

Get the popcorn.

item.title: NFL kickoff game preview: Why the under 44.5 is the play in Seahawks-Patriots rematch
item.description: Drake Maye and the Patriots host Sam Darnold's Seahawks in a Super Bowl rematch as both teams navigate major offseason roster changes tonight.
item.content:encoded:
After months of waiting, and me writing roughly 20,000+ words about the upcoming NFL season, with a preview for every team, we have finally reached the opening night of the new NFL year. As usual, it starts with the Super Bowl Champion starting their title defense at home. This year, on NBC, we get the New England Patriots taking on the Seattle Seahawks in a Super Bowl rematch.

The Patriots didn’t take the offseason off after getting to the championship game. They were aggressive in upgrading their offense now that they believe in Drake Maye. They lost Stefon Diggs, but they added AJ Brown, who is still a very good receiver, even if he wasn’t very happy with the Philadelphia Eagles. The bigger offseason story surrounded their head coach, Mike Vrabel, and his alleged affair with reporter Diana Russini.

How all of these distractions and changes come into play will be determined in this game. I think this team has enough talent to battle for the division again. However, this year is different from last season. Last year, the Patriots were a surprise, Maye was an MVP candidate, and the team shocked the league. This year a tougher schedule awaits, and Maye, in my opinion, had the best season of his career last year.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Seahawks were a buzz saw in the playoffs. They destroyed pretty much everyone, with the exception of the Los Angeles Rams. They completely dismantled and destroyed the San Francisco 49ers in their first playoff game, and then they outlasted the Rams 31-27. In the Super Bowl, they beat the Patriots 29-13. It was a fairly boring game, unfortunately. The Seahawks were never really in jeopardy of losing the game and were up 12-0 after three quarters, scoring just field goals.

Even with a somewhat exciting fourth quarter, it was too little too late for the Patriots, and the Seahawks hoisted the trophy. The Seahawks lost their Super Bowl MVP running back, and they lost their offensive coordinator. That could change things up a bit, as Sam Darnold saw a lot of success last year under him. Defensively, the team should still be strong, but this is a tough division, so we will see how it goes.

Defending Super Bowl Champions are 13-5 in the NFL Kickoff Game. If you look at how they perform overall in the first week, typically they win about 70-80% of the games over the past two decades. Teams that lose the Super Bowl are 10-15. However, they have been a bit better over the past 13 years, going 8-5.

Both of these teams should be carried by their defense. That isn’t to say they have no offense; I just think their defenses will be better earlier in the year. We have Maye, who struggled mightily against this defense, and won’t be great tonight. Then we have Darnold with a new offensive coordinator. I am going to back the under 44.5 in this one. I do think the Seahawks win and cover the -3, but I’ll just back the under. Note that the Seahawks safety Ty Okada is out and Nick Emmanwori is questionable. That could open up the field a bit for the Patriots.

item.title: Proposal would pay homeowners 'data center dividends' to counter growing backlash
item.description: Think tank proposes sharing data center tax revenue with local residents through direct payments, tax credits or scholarships
item.content:encoded:
As opposition to artificial intelligence data centers spreads across rural America, one group is proposing "data center dividends" to counter the backlash by allowing residents to share directly in the wealth generated by the technology hubs.

A new report from the Bitcoin Policy Institute, a think tank based in Washington, D.C., proposes that data center dividends are a model that would return part of the property tax revenue generated by AI data centers directly to households living in the communities that host the data centers, potentially providing annual payments of between about $4,500 and $8,900 per household without creating new taxes or increasing costs for developers.

"Every American deserves to benefit from the AI boom," Sam Lyman, head of research at the nonprofit, told Fox News Digital. "It can't just be the developers in Silicon Valley who are becoming wealthy from this revolution. It needs to be the Americans who are building the county infrastructure that makes these data centers possible in the first place."

The proposal comes as opposition to data centers intensifies nationwide, fomented over the past year by a network of socialists and communist nonprofits funded by a tech tycoon, Neville Roy Singham, living in Shanghai, supporting the Chinese Communist Party and a "new world order" promulgated by Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The opposition has widened to conservatives and centrists, with the report noting that Americans are now more likely to oppose a data center in their community than a nuclear power plant.

In a poll earlier this year, Gallup found that 71% of Americans oppose construction of an AI data center in their area, while only 53% oppose a nearby nuclear plant. The report says local data center moratoriums have exploded from six in 2024 to 59 last year and 294 last month.

Over the past year, groups in the Singham network – including the Party for Socialism and Liberation, the People's Forum, CodePink and BreakThrough News – have opposed data centers and also Flock surveillance cameras with aggressive media campaigns, elevating China as a technological powerhouse and denigrating any developments by U.S. technology companies.

"These influence actions are cognitive warfare. Foreign actors don't need Americans to become pro-China," Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity at the National Security Agency, recently told Fox News Digital. "They need Americans to argue for the outcomes Beijing wants. And a free society that can't build the power and govern the advanced technology is going to wind up renting it from the adversary, read the PRC, that doesn't share its own values. And that scares me as an American."

Lyman said the political problem is that many Americans believe technology companies are reaping the benefits of the AI boom while local communities bear the costs. The propaganda campaigns by the pro-China groups are promoting that message by describing tech executives as "oligarchs" and "imperialists." One constant message in the campaigns is "People Over Profits."

"I really think that data center dividends will reverse the momentum in the data center debate, because suddenly every American who lives in these counties where data centers might be built recognizes that he or she can have a material stake in the AI economy," said Lyman, a former senior advisor and speechwriter for Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Polling cited in the report found that 73% of Americans believe the costs of data center construction outweigh the benefits, while voters overwhelmingly believe AI will primarily enrich executives and business owners rather than workers.

Rather than creating a new tax, the proposal would redirect a portion of property tax revenue that counties already collect from data centers. "Data center dividends can ensure that rural Americans rise in the age of AI alongside the engineers developing this technology," the report notes.

Under the model, counties would first continue funding schools, roads, police and other essential services. After those obligations are met, local communities would return a portion of remaining revenue directly to residents through annual checks, direct deposits, tax credits, utility bill credits or permanent investment funds. The report emphasizes that the dividends would be financed entirely from existing tax revenue, meaning developers wouldn't pay any additional taxes.

The report estimates that a single one-gigawatt AI data center could generate enough tax revenue to provide households in a typical rural county between $4,500 and $8,900 annually in a "data center dividend," depending on how much revenue local governments dedicate to dividends after paying for public services.

The estimate is based on tax collections from Loudoun County, Va., one of the nation's largest data center hubs. Loudoun collected about $685 million in personal property taxes on data center computer equipment in fiscal year 2024. Dividing those collections by the county's data center electrical load produced an estimate of roughly $165 million in annual property tax revenue per gigawatt of AI infrastructure, researchers estimated.

The report cites new policies in West Feliciana Parish, La., where policymakers are attempting to spread new-found wealth. The parish expects a Hut 8 AI campus to generate about $90 million annually, more than tripling its current budget, according to estimates. Earlier this year, Louisiana lawmakers passed Act 434, allowing local officials to provide property tax credits funded by the new revenue, although lawmakers removed an earlier proposal that would have authorized direct cash payments.

If the cash provision had remained, the report estimates households could have received about $5,600 annually if one-quarter of the revenue were distributed, or $11,200 annually if half the revenue were shared with residents after funding government services.

In another example, Alaska has a "Permanent Fund," or state-owned investment account that collects part of Alaska's revenues from oil produced on state land, invests it in stocks, bonds and real estate, and disburses part of the returns to residents as an annual dividend.

The report outlines several options communities could adopt.

Lyman argues that direct payments create stronger public support than simply lowering taxes or expanding government spending because residents would see the benefit. "I think a lot that opposition is born from the fact that many Americans feel left out of the AI boom. They feel like this economic revolution is taking place without them," said Lyman, noting, "What data center dividends do... is they give every American in rural America a share in the material prosperity that is taking place with artificial intelligence."

The report notes that rural counties possess two scarce assets essential for AI development – land and abundant power – and argues those communities should share directly in the economic gains generated by the AI buildout.

item.title: Sandra Bullock's wake-up call that changed everything during late partner Bryan Randall’s illness
item.description: Sandra Bullock reveals her sister's urgent warning forced her to confront the hidden toll of caregiving during partner Bryan Randall's private ALS battle.
item.content:encoded:
A sobering warning from Sandra Bullock’s sister became a wake-up call for the actress as she quietly navigated her late partner Bryan Randall’s battle with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

Bullock reflected on how caring for Randall through his illness forced her to recognize her own limits – and ultimately ask for help after years of putting others first.

"I'm always a caretaker," she said during an appearance on "Good Hang with Amy Poehler." "Always. And I learned that I didn't take care of the person that was taking care of everybody else. And that was a big wake-up call for me. And I'm not good at asking for help, but I needed help and I needed to ask it in a way that was safe."

SANDRA BULLOCK SAYS BRYAN RANDALL WAS ILL FOR 'HALF OF OUR RELATIONSHIP' AS SHE OPENS UP ABOUT HIS DEATH

"The Blind Side" star said she was grateful for the people who stepped in to help guide her through the difficult time. She also credited her sister with ringing a much-needed alarm, warning that she needed to start taking care of herself so she could continue being there for her children, Louis and Laila.

Bullock said her sister warned her: "If you do not start taking care of you, something’s gonna happen to you."

Bullock said the experience opened her eyes to the toll caregiving can take on those who put their own needs aside.

"The caretaker world is absolutely underserved," Bullock said. "I did what I had to do in the situation I was in."

"I didn't want to say anything out of turn on what anyone else experienced within that situation, because everyone is experiencing something, their own journey with that," she explained. "There's so much to the story that would be of service. But my story, my slice of pie – and me and the kids, you know – that's all we can speak about."

Bullock revealed her minimal history as a caregiver during a recent episode of the "SmartLess" podcast.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I'm a very good planner with illness because my father was ill and had horrible accidents and my mother had cancer – I feel like I'm very comfortable in a setting where someone is ill," she told the hosts. "It doesn't scare me, not the illness itself. It doesn't scare me. I can see and be around just about anything."

Randall had been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease, amid the COVID-19 pandemic and requested Bullock not make the news public. He died on Aug. 5, 2023. He was 57.

"I wasn't allowed to speak about it," she revealed on the podcast. "That was the request, and I honored it."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

But honoring Randall’s wishes came with a personal cost for Bullock.

"I know why he asked me not to... it isolated me in the process and, plus, the entire world was locked in with the pandemic," she said. "He was ill for half of our relationship and the diagnosis came almost at the same time with the cloak of the pandemic."

Bullock admitted that "not talking for a while was good," but the physical illness coupled with "the mental health aspect" created a "trifecta that was pretty dark."

Fox News Digital's Tracy Wright contributed to this report.

item.title: Fmr Biden ambassador blames Trump for Canada playing 'footsie' with China
item.description: Former U.S. Ambassador David L. Cohen says Canada is playing "footsie" with China on trade as Trump's hardline policies push allies toward new deals.
item.content:encoded:
Former U.S. Ambassador to Canada David L. Cohen is blaming the Trump administration's hardline trade pressure for pushing Ottawa into engaging with China.

"I think Canada has tentatively tried to play some footsie with China that the Trump administration may not be happy with," Cohen, who served as President Joe Biden’s ambassador to Canada from 2021 to 2025, said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"There is a discomfort with that," Cohen says, while arguing that it is ultimately Canada's reflex to sentiment against President Donald Trump – particularly his hardline trade policies and rhetoric about the neighbor to the north being a "51st state."

VANCE SAYS CANADA FRIENDLIER TO CHINA ON TRADE THAN TO US: 'INSANITY'

"One of downsides of the aggressive Trump administration treatment of Canada and many other allies and partners is that the irony is that those policies are pushing those countries to at least consider broader and larger deals with China, which of course is wholly inconsistent with a major thrust of President Trump's international trade policy," Cohen continued. "So, how that shakes out, it's all a matter of degree and balance.

"But I think there's no doubt that the aggressiveness of the Trump administration positions has caused many countries to at least reevaluate whether there are additional deals that can be made with China."

The comments come as U.S.-Canada trade tensions spiral after negotiations collapsed last month. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday accused Washington of seeking dependence rather than partnership.

"The most fundamental issue is that the cumulative U.S. demands revealed that they wanted us to become even more reliant on them, not less," Carney said. "In too many areas, they wanted dependency, not a true economic partnership."

TRUMP TAUNTS CANADA ON RENAMING LAKE ONTARIO THE 'LAKE AMERICA' AMID RISING BORDER TRADE RIFT

Notably, the fallout comes just weeks before Chinese dictator Xi Jinping makes an historic trip to the White House to talk trade – something that never happened during the Biden administration despite Biden's onetime quip before the COVID-19 pandemic that "China's not bad folks."

Vice President JD Vance, speaking in Maine last month, accused Canada of giving Chinese goods better treatment than products from American northern border states.

"They treat Chinese goods more fairly than they do the goods that come from the people of Maine: It’s insanity," Vance said. "And what we’ve said to Canada is, ‘Stop it.’"

Cohen, however, was careful not to cast Canada as blameless in the trade feud. He admitted U.S. dairy farmers have legitimate complaints about Canada’s tariff-rate quota system, saying the issue has frustrated administrations of both parties for years.

WHITE HOUSE EXPOSES ‘TRANSSHIPMENT SCAM’ COSTING US UP TO $26B, POINTS FINGER AT CHINA

"This is one of the totally legitimate trade issues that exists between the United States and Canada," Cohen said. "There is contention there that is hurting American dairy farmers. Yes, I will be honest and clear about that."

"That tension existed under Joe Biden. Was he able to solve that problem? No," he added. "It was something that was discussed and discussed more than once. We just never got there."

Cohen, supportive of Trump's "substance" on trade talks but not the "style," did credit Trump for replacing NAFTA with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, calling USMCA a "terrific deal" that improved continental trade.

TRUMP TRADE CHIEF WARNS CANADA WALKED AWAY FROM 'THE BEST DEAL' TO TRIGGER 50% U.S. TARIFFS

"I gave President Trump a lot of credit for that because it was a much better deal than NAFTA," Cohen said. "I think he deserves credit for that."

"I do push back at times on some of the rhetoric that President Trump has chosen to use, not necessarily the substance, but maybe the style that he sometimes uses to pursue his substance," he added.

"There are such fundamental differences on the substance of President Trump’s trade policy that I think the treatment of President Trump is different than the treatment of President Biden," Cohen observed. "But when professional negotiators were in the room, they seemed to have been making a lot of progress."

Cohen believes the two sides need to return to professional negotiators, arguing that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Canadian officials had shown they could discuss difficult issues before the talks broke down.

TRUMP MUST CLOSE THE BACK DOOR CHINA USES TO EXPLOIT NORTH AMERICAN TRADE

"I have an enormous amount of respect for U.S. Trade Representative Greer," Cohen said. "He is the ultimate professional trade negotiator, which is why he’s in that job. He didn’t get there by accident. President Trump put him in that job."

By contrast, Cohen said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – who was on the call that Friday night in August when talks broke down at the 11th hour – needs to stay in his lane.

"Secretary of Commerce Lutnick, with all due respect, is not a professional negotiator," Cohen said. "That’s not the Commerce secretary’s job. It’s USTR’s job to negotiate trade deals with other countries."

Lutnick has suggested in interviews about the infamous breakdown in talks that Canadians' politics are at play in keeping Carney from cutting a deal with Trump, a man the provincial leaders and Canadian public have long been disenchanted with.

TRUMP TRADE CHIEF REVEALS WHAT PRECEDED CANADA WALKING AWAY FROM 'BEST DEAL IN THE WORLD'

"Friday at 4 o'clock, the Canadians call: They start adding crazy ideas to the mix," Lutnick said recently. "So, I said to one of the ministers, 'Are you actually trying to blow this up?' And his answer to me was, 'I'm not allowed to say that.' And they blew it up for political reasons only."

Cohen said of Lutnick's account that "until proven otherwise, I take every senior government official at his word, period," and that he has "no way of knowing whether that is true or not."

But, he admitted, Carney taking the nearly finished trade deal back to the provinces did not go over well – particularly amid his rising popularity among Canadians for being an anti-Trump force – because "the premiers of the provinces have more sway in federal policy than most governors do in federal policy."

CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT

"It appears that Canada made the decision that the deal that was being offered was not a deal that they could accept," Cohen said. "He may have made a judgment that although he and his team had pushed this deal as far as they could, and that it was, in his eyes, as good a deal as he was going to get at that point, that he could not sell that politically in Canada."

"That’s not the same as saying that he was walking away for political reasons," Cohen added. "It’s just the nature of a big, complex negotiation."

TRUMP'S CANADA TARIFF FIGHT REACHES CRITICAL POINT AS HOUSE GOP SUMMONS TRADE CHIEF

Ultimately, Cohen said the breakdown between the closest allies and trade partners in the world will be a story long told.

"There are going to be books written about what caused the negotiations to fall apart," he said. "But independent of all the dialogue about that: There is no dispute that these professional negotiators were able to have a civil relationship and talk about really different difficult substantive issues out of the eyes and the ears of the press and with full respect for each other and for the countries. item.title: $54M CodePink-linked foundation shut down in California pops up at ramshackle Miami home
item.description: Arc of Justice, led by CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin, lost its California registration and resurfaced as a Florida nonprofit at a Miami duplex.
item.content:encoded:
A far-left foundation that bankrolled CodePink and recently reported $54.6 million in assets before being shut down by California regulators has resurfaced at a ramshackle Miami home.

Arc of Justice, led by CodePink co-founder Susan Medea Benjamin, lost its charitable registration after years of failing to file required financial paperwork with California. But what appears to be the same nonprofit is now registered at a small, single-story house owned by Benjamin's longtime partner and fellow activist, Tighe Barry, documents viewed by Fox News Digital show.

The sequence of events raises questions about why it fell out of compliance in California.

HOUSE PANEL SUBPOENAS 3 LEFT-WING GROUPS IN PROBE OF $39M TIED TO MARXIST TYCOON NEVILLE SINGHAM

Arc of Justice has poured millions of dollars into left-wing and progressive activist organizations over the years, including CodePink, Global Exchange, the Alliance for Global Justice and the National Iranian American Council, according to IRS filings. Federal tax returns provided to Fox News Digital by Arc of Justice's attorney show the California foundation's assets grew from $51.4 million at the end of 2023 to $54.6 million at the end of 2024, while it continued distributing millions of dollars in grants.

CodePink has campaigned against U.S. policy toward China and Cuba and has been accused by congressional investigators of promoting Chinese Communist Party interests — allegations the group has denied.

Benjamin, who has been a political activist for decades and has often disrupted congressional hearings, co-founded CodePink with Jodie Evans, the wife of Shanghai-based Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, whose funding network has come under congressional and federal scrutiny over alleged foreign influence and the use of tax-exempt organizations.

Now it’s Arc of Justice’s finances that are coming under the microscope.

"It's pretty unusual. Most private foundations are fairly scrupulous on their compliance efforts," Patrick Sternal, a former IRS official who specialized in tax-exempt organizations, told Fox News Digital. "So it's unusual for a private foundation with that much in the bank to fall out of compliance and to be suspended."

The California Attorney General's Office, led by Democrat Rob Bonta, revoked Arc of Justice's charitable registration in January 2025 after it failed to submit required annual filings with the state for 2020 through 2024. The foundation had already been suspended for more than a year before the revocation. The state Attorney General's Office told Fox News Digital that Arc of Justice had continually failed to respond to the registry's delinquency and suspension notices before its registration was revoked.

Under the revocation, Arc of Justice had 30 days to provide the state with an accounting of its charitable assets and was barred from distributing or spending them without the attorney general's prior written approval.

The years of noncompliance culminated in another notice from California regulators on June 19, 2026, reiterating the outstanding asset-accounting requirement and warning that Arc of Justice couldn’t distribute or spend charitable assets without the attorney general's written approval.

The notice said Arc of Justice would also have to provide regulators with enough information to assure the state that there had been "no loss of charitable assets" if it sought to have its registration reinstated. The Network Contagion Research Institute previously detailed Arc of Justice's regulatory problems in a May report examining the foundation's finances and activities.

FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS

David Levitt, an attorney representing Arc of Justice, said the foundation has submitted filings seeking reinstatement with California regulators.

The Attorney General's Office told Fox News Digital on Sept. 3, 2026, that it had not received the required accounting of Arc's charitable assets. At the time, Arc was listed as "REVOKED" and "PAST DUE." As of Sept. 9, its registration remained "REVOKED," while its reporting status had changed to "IN REVIEW."

California's reinstatement rules require a revoked charity to explain why it failed to comply with reporting requirements and respond to Registry notices.

Laurie Styron, CEO and executive director of nonprofit watchdog CharityWatch, said Arc's substantial assets made the compliance failures difficult to explain.

"A foundation with tens of millions of dollars in charitable assets certainly has the resources to comply with basic reporting requirements," she said.

Fox News Digital asked Levitt to provide documentation of the reinstatement filings and to explain specifically why Arc of Justice failed to make the required California filings in the first place. He had not responded to those questions by publication time.

California's latest compliance notice to Arc of Justice came just six weeks after a new Arc of Justice surfaced in Florida.

On May 8, Barry and other people associated with the original foundation incorporated a new nonprofit bearing the same name in the Little River neighborhood in North Miami.

The timing raised obvious questions: Was the California foundation moving to Florida after its charitable registration was revoked, and what was happening to its assets?

The Attorney General's Office told Fox News Digital it had not received notice from Arc of Justice of any planned transfer, merger or dissolution and had not approved any transfer of the foundation's assets.

Levitt told Fox News Digital that the Florida corporation was created as a "placeholder" while Arc considered relocating its operations from California, but the move was never completed. He said the California corporation was never formally wound down, no assets were transferred and the Florida entity "holds no assets and has conducted no business."

"Arc of Justice, the California nonprofit corporation, currently still holds the assets," Levitt said, adding that they remain professionally managed "in the same accounts they have been in for years."

Levitt subsequently provided Fox News Digital with financial documentation that independently verified that the California foundation continues to hold the assets.

The Miami address wasn't new. The original Arc of Justice had been using Barry's property on its federal tax filings since at least 2017, even as it remained incorporated in California.

Questions have also emerged about the original foundation's federal filings.

Arc of Justice's Forms 990-PF for 2023 and 2024 were not publicly available in the IRS database when Fox News Digital searched for them. Levitt subsequently provided Fox News Digital with copies of both returns.

According to Levitt, Arc of Justice's accountant said both returns had been paper-filed and electronically filed, although Fox News Digital has not independently verified when the IRS received or accepted them.

Benjamin was adamant in a phone interview with Fox News Digital that Arc of Justice had filed its returns every year.

"I'm 100% positive. We have filed the 990s every single year," Benjamin said. She also told Fox News Digital she would make sure the missing returns were provided, which they subsequently were.

Benjamin was less certain about the foundation's California regulatory problems, saying she had moved to Florida and that "the lawyer knows more than I do."

After reviewing the newly produced returns, Sternal said the documents showed Arc of Justice's accountant had at least made an effort to file them, but said questions remained over whether and when they were actually submitted.

"Maybe they are trying to get back into compliance with the IRS," Sternal said. "They still have a lot of clean up to do with California."

Styron similarly said determining when the returns were actually filed was critical to assessing Arc of Justice's compliance. She noted that IRS and state databases can lag behind submissions but said delays of several years would be unusual.

"It would be tough to say more without knowing when forms were signed and filed," Styron said.

While the new records accounted for the foundation's assets and provided the previously unavailable returns, questions remained over when the federal returns were actually filed.

Styron also said Arc of Justice's explanation for creating the Florida nonprofit did not absolve the California foundation's board of its responsibility to file the active organization's required forms on time.

Meanwhile, Sternal, who is now a nonprofit tax attorney at law firm Holtzman Vogel who advises nonprofit and tax-exempt organizations, said there is nothing wrong or unusual about forming a nonprofit in another state. What raises questions, he said, is whether the new Florida organization is intended to take over the original foundation or its assets — a move that would trigger additional legal requirements.

"It's not so easy," Sternal said. "It can be done, it's possible, but there are a lot of hoops that they have to jump through."

Because Arc of Justice remained a California corporation, Sternal said it would have to work with California's attorney general before transferring funds to another organization or moving the foundation out of state.

Along with the new Florida corporation bearing the same Arc of Justice name and Miami address used by the embattled California foundation, two of its three officers also held positions with the original organization.

Maya Danaher, Benjamin's daughter and former treasurer of the original Arc of Justice, is president of the new Florida corporation.

Jonathan Raggett, who served as secretary of the original foundation, is now its treasurer.

Benjamin served as president of the original California foundation but is not listed as an officer of the new Florida corporation.

Meanwhile, Benjamin's longtime partner, Barry, was not listed as an officer of the original foundation but serves as secretary of the new organization. He is also listed as incorporating Arc of Justice in Florida and serves as its registered agent.

Its stated goal is blunt: "WE ARE HERE TO SUPPORT SOCIAL JUSTICE NON PROFITS," according to the articles of incorporation.

All three officers list the Miami house as their address — a 1,334-square-foot Miami duplex owned by Barry, property records show.

When Fox News Digital visited last month, the small, turquoise-blue, single-story house sat partially obscured by thick palms and tropical plants behind a weathered, multicolored wooden fence.

Fading artwork of colorful cats, pigs, flowers, hearts and peace symbols covered the fence, including a pink pig holding a "ONE LOVE" sign. A large "PEACE" poster hung on the house, while a turquoise-shaded canopy stretched across the property.

Two campaign signs for Democrat Kendrick Meek Jr., who unsuccessfully ran in the Democratic primary election for Florida's 24th Congressional District, stood outside.

Google Street View images from 2022 show the property in brighter colors before the paint faded and vegetation obscured parts of the fence.

The images also show a small white van with its front bumper missing parked outside, with "CODEPINK" written across its side in pink marker along with the Spanish words "Cuba vive y trabaja" — "Cuba lives and works."

The van was not visible when Fox News Digital visited.

The house's number was painted vertically on the weathered front gate — the same address listed by the original California foundation and the newly incorporated Florida Arc of Justice.

SUBPOENAED PRO-CHINA OUTLET DEFENDS ITSELF ON DEMOCRACY NOW!, WHICH PAID SINGHAM-FOUNDED COMPANY MILLIONS

Arc of Justice was formerly known as The Benjamin Fund, Inc., with California corporate records showing the foundation formally changed its name in November 2019.

Its fortune was built largely on Benjamin family money.

Benjamin's father, Alvin Benjamin, was a prominent Long Island real estate developer who founded The Benjamin Companies in the early 1960s. The Benjamin Fund's initial 2003 IRS return shows he contributed a partnership interest valued at $683,715 to the foundation, with Medea Susan Benjamin serving as president.

Much larger contributions followed. In 2010, the estate of Benjamin's mother, Rose Benjamin, contributed $10,863,060, according to the foundation's IRS filing. Five years later, the Estate of Alvin Benjamin contributed another $15 million, followed by another $8,603,450 in 2019.

The foundation's wealth also grew through its investments. In 2020, Arc of Justice reported $12,344,501 in unrealized gains on securities, helping push its year-end assets to nearly $40 million.

Medea Benjamin — identified as Susan Benjamin on the filing — personally contributed $1 million to Arc of Justice in 2022, listing the Miami house as her address.

The foundation subsequently became a vehicle for funding activist organizations, including Global Exchange, the advocacy group Benjamin co-founded with her then-husband, Kevin Danaher. The organization remains active today, with Danaher still serving on its board, according to its 2024 Form 990.

Benjamin later co-founded CodePink in 2002 with Evans and has remained one of the anti-war group's most prominent activists and public faces.

Arc of Justice would go on to pour substantial sums into CodePink, including $251,500 in 2020 and $355,350 in 2022, according to the foundation's IRS filings.

The newly obtained returns show that Arc of Justice gave CodePink $277,580 in 2023 and another $350,000 in 2024.

CodePink has itself come under federal scrutiny. Benjamin traveled to Cuba in March with fellow CodePink co-founder Evans and far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker as part of a roughly 170-person convoy to the communist-run island.

Benjamin later confirmed that the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control, which enforces U.S. sanctions against Cuba, sent CodePink a detailed inquiry seeking information about the trip's financing, logistics, participants and activities.

Benjamin said the group brought about $600,000 worth of humanitarian aid to Cuba and described the Treasury inquiry as "serious," while also calling it an "intimidation tactic."

Evans and a network of nonprofits funded by her husband, Singham, have also come under congressional and federal scrutiny.

Singham, an American tech entrepreneur who sold his software company ThoughtWorks for an estimated $785 million in 2017 and now lives in Shanghai, has directed at least $278 million into six core nonprofits that Fox News Digital previously reported promote socialist, communist and pro-China causes as part of a broader international network of media organizations, activist groups and think tanks.

CodePink is one of those nonprofits.

The congressional investigation remains ongoing, while Singham is separately under federal criminal investigation. Neither Singham nor CodePink has been charged with wrongdoing in connection with the investigations described here.

Florida officials confirmed the new Arc of Justice was created as a Florida nonprofit on May 8, 2026, rather than simply registering the existing California corporation in the state.

"That entity is on our records as a Domestic Nonprofit corporation. It is a Florida entity," Florida Department of State regulatory specialist LaCori Brown told Fox News Digital.

The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services separately told Fox News Digital that the new Arc of Justice isn’t currently registered to solicit charitable contributions in the state and has not applied for a charitable solicitation registration or exemption.

The department also said it hasn’t received any filings identifying assets transferred from the California Arc of Justice to the new Florida corporation nor any complaints, referrals or regulatory inquiries concerning the new organization.

Sternal stressed that the available records don’t establish that Arc of Justice's assets were misappropriated or improperly used. He said the foundation's years of California noncompliance remained highly unusual.

"This organization with this large endowment has simply fallen off the radar, as it were, with its filings, with its compliance with California," Sternal said.

"Those don't belong to the officers and directors of the foundation. Those belong to the foundation," Sternal said. "They must be used for public charitable purposes."

Levitt said Arc of Justice's board is still considering moving the foundation out of California and potentially establishing two separate charitable vehicles so the foundation's founder and its officers and directors can pursue separate charitable activities.

For now, the original Arc of Justice remains a California corporation and continues to hold its assets, while the future of the newly incorporated Florida organization remains unsettled.

item.title: Armed man accused of lunging at Ohio Dem candidate avoids felonies as prosecutor reveals key evidence
item.description: Patrick Havas' own video is the only footage of the Canfield Fair incident after Amy Acton's camp allegedly asked people to stop recording it.
item.content:encoded:
The man who allegedly stormed toward Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton at a recent fair will not face felony charges, the county prosecutor leading the case told reporters Tuesday.

The only video investigators currently have of the incident was recorded by the suspect, Patrick Havas, leaving authorities with little video evidence, Mahoning County Prosecutor Lynn Maro said. 

"The information we've received is that the Acton camp requested individuals stop recording shortly before this incident occurred," Maro told reporters on Tuesday.

"So, at this point, the only video we have is the defendant’s. And what's that showing certainly doesn't support filing felony charges."

PISTOL-PACKING MAN KNOCKS OVER FAIRGOERS FORCING HIS WAY TOWARD OHIO GOVERNOR CANDIDATE AMY ACTON, POLICE SAY

Patrick Havas was intercepted by Ohio Highway Patrol officers after allegedly knocking over multiple fairgoers as he ran toward Acton at a tent at the Canfield Fair while armed with a Taser and two firearms.

He was initially booked on two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct, all misdemeanors. An inducing panic charge was added Tuesday at his arraignment, bringing the total to four misdemeanor counts. Havas pleaded not guilty.

Maro said the tape showed Havas "walking into the tent" where Acton was, and "calling out her name" before executive protection unit officers from Ohio Highway Patrol interrupted him.

"Then, his phone is either dropped or tossed, and that’s all we have," Maro said.

RAMASWAMY TORCHES DEM RIVAL OVER 'OUTRAGEOUS' COVID-19 CLAIM: 'SPEWING LIES'

"There's never any close contact with the governor, never gets near her — sorry, ‘candidate for governor’," she added.

Fox News Digital reached out to Maro for comment and to obtain a copy of the video in question. An official who picked up the phone at her office said Maro was out but would be checking messages.

A reporter for the NBC affiliate tweeted that their network had also attempted to obtain the video but that officials said they would not be releasing it as part of their "active investigation."

Fox News Digital also reached out to the Acton campaign for additional comment, as well as details around the reported request that people stop filming Acton just before the encounter.

"While attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr. Acton, injuring multiple people. Dr. Acton and Eric are grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured," Acton campaign communications director Addie Bullock said in a separate statement.

"This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr. Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another."

An Ohio judge ordered Havas to not speak to the press, according to Youngstown’s NBC affiliate, and Havas has been placed under a $5,000 bond and forced to surrender any weaponry in his possession.

Havas is a local to that region of Ohio. He was arrested in 2008 on petty theft and disorderly conduct charges, according to Newsweek. The theft charge was later dismissed after he pleaded no contest to disorderly conduct. He was accused of stealing several movies from a supermarket, including the James Bond film "Casino Royale."

Acton faces Republican entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy in November, as Gov. Mike DeWine is term-limited. DeWine’s lieutenant, former Ohio State Football coach Jim Tressel, declined to run for the office.

item.title: Reporter’s Notebook: 9/11 is just a history chapter for a new generation of Americans
item.description: A quarter century after 9/11, one-third of Americans alive that day are gone, and the memories of Sept. 11, 2001, grow increasingly faded.
item.content:encoded:
It’s faded.

Not from decay. Not from neglect. It’s simply the passage of time.

The memories are vague. Elusive. Distant. And some who lived it are simply no longer here.

Roughly one-third of all Americans who were alive on 9/11 aren’t around anymore to observe the 25th anniversary of that abominable day. And so the recollections of Sept. 11, 2001, are diluted.

NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS

To some, Sept. 11 is just another day. But it’s something different for those who weren’t around to live and breathe the horror.

To many, 9/11 is like Pearl Harbor Day. Lots of people know about it. They understand it’s what triggered the U.S.’s entry into World War II. But they can’t quite explain much more.

The same with other historical-shifting moments. Aug. 6 and 9, 1945 — the days the U.S. bombed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, effectively ending World War II. Nov. 22, 1963 — the day a gunman mowed down President John F. Kennedy Jr. in Dallas.

A lot of people remember the Space Shuttle Challenger exploding. But few could tell you that it happened on Jan. 28, 1986.

The quintessence of 9/11 is the date. Kind of like July 4th. A bit like Jan. 6 and the Capitol riot. However, we were told on Sept. 11, 2001, that things would never be the same. But how can those who didn’t experience it understand what "the same" was like if they never lived it?

Just last month, a relative of mine who soon turns 26 asked, "What it was like to fly before 9/11?"

I can regale you with stories about myself and a rag-tag group of high school friends, driving to the Cincinnati airport, clearing security and just wandering around the Delta gates, "hanging out" back in the mid-1980s.

No ticket. No questions asked. Just a visit to Cinnabon.

But the "before times" question about 9/11 is a broader conversation. It’s not just about "what changed" when you take off your shoes and bustle through security to fly.

LIZ PEEK: WE CANNOT LET THE LEFT REWRITE WHAT HAPPENED ON 9/11

A nine-and-a-half-foot-tall plaque hangs in the East Front vestibule of the U.S. Capitol near the Rotunda. It commemorates Flight 93, which crashed near Shanksville, Pa., on 9/11.

It took a few years, but the U.S. intelligence services finally determined that the fourth plane was bound for the U.S. Capitol. That’s where Todd Beamer and a cadre of everyday Americans voted (mind you, at 35,000 feet) to commandeer a drinks cart and rush the cockpit in an effort to seize control of the plane.

"Let’s roll!" Beamer was overheard saying on a cellphone as they charged down the aisle. That two-word phrase became a battle cry for a nation as it waged the war on terrorism.

The Boeing 757 hurtled toward Washington at 563 mph. It was 20 minutes out from the federal city when the plane crashed, upside down, in the Pennsylvania countryside.

Shanksville is now one of those places forever notched into American history. A place not as famous, say, as Gettysburg or Jamestown, but not a footnote, either. Shanksville is part of the vernacular like Shiloh, Seneca Falls, Kent.

People might know that something historic happened there. But they aren’t exactly sure what.

Scores of markers dot the U.S. Capitol, denoting important things from yesteryear. Wander into Statuary Hall in the Capitol and you’ll find the desk locations of eight presidents who served in the House. But the spot where President Franklin Pierce once sat just seems like an historical annotation. Pierce toiled there nearly two centuries ago. And he’s hardly prominent among American chief executives.

There’s a plaque just outside the Old Supreme Court chamber. It tells the story of how Samuel B. Morse sent the first electronic message from that room to Baltimore over a wire in 1844. "What hath God wrought!" reads the plaque, commemorating Morse’s transmission. That event christened the age of near-instant communication – now ubiquitous in the form of news alerts and TikTok videos appearing instantly in the palms of our hands.

But that plaque in the Capitol’s East Front vestibule doesn’t memorialize something that happened there. It marks something that didn’t happen there.

The plaque reads that the actions of the 40 passengers and crew "not only saved countless lives, but may have saved the U.S. Capitol from destruction."

In other words, this global citadel to democracy with its ivory dome might not pierce the Washington skyline were it not for a plane that crashed 167 miles away.

Shanksville. Shiloh. Seneca Falls. Kent.

TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE

I’ve driven the Pennsylvania Turnpike past Somerset for decades now. That’s where the signs direct you north 10 miles to the Flight 93 National Memorial. I budgeted time into my travels to visit the memorial on one frigid, windy morning a few Februarys ago. Inside, you stand at a vista, staring downhill into a small ravine and tree line where the plane crashed.

On that morning, I couldn’t help but notice there was no wildlife to be seen or heard. No deer. No birds chirping.

A disturbing silence.

Perhaps it was the billowing wind of that frosty morning. Maybe the snow. But I noticed no footprints gouging the crisp snowpack.

It was almost as though the animals were aware of something. Dare I say understood what happened in this field a quarter-century ago. Perhaps the local fauna stayed hushed out of reverence for those who perished. A tribute to their heroism, saving the U.S. Capitol.

Or perhaps it was something else.

Maybe the creatures were so reserved because of the malevolence which was also on board Flight 93. One can only speculate that the animals remain hushed because of the peculiar unease enveloping the place. Even on a crisp but blustery winter morning.

Shanksville is a burial ground. And in a few more decades or even a hundred years, those who visit there will walk the paths or peer out over the panorama, trying to grasp the scope of what unfolded there on 9/11.

FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE

You can visit Gettysburg and Antietam and do that now. But much is left to the imagination. Perhaps embroidered by what was picked up in a history class. Augmented by a marker or description on a bronze plaque.

In another quarter-century, there will be even fewer people around who remember 9/11. Another 25 after that and many of those still living might be infirm. Confined to wheelchairs. The final generation of messengers who can speak firsthand about what happened that day. Kind of like when honor flights descend on Washington to visit the World War II Memorial on the National Mall.

It’s just the passage of time.

The plaque inside the Capitol will continue to tell the story. And in many ways, just the fact that the Capitol remains standing tells the story, too. Its presence attests to the bravery that manifested itself somewhere over eastern Ohio and is interred in a western Pennsylvania clearing.

We know this now. Even though some of what we recall is faded.

But the memories and understanding of the significance will naturally calcify. Details will grow hazy. People will know the date 9/11. But it may just be that — a date. Like Pearl Harbor Day.

President Franklin Delano Roosevelt referred to Dec. 7, 1941, as "a date which will live infamy."

9/11 will live in infamy. But it’s unclear how that date will live in the minds of Americans.

item.title: Amazon cargo jet pilot reportedly told wife, 'My career is over' shortly after deadly crash
item.description: A pilot from the Amazon cargo plane crash at Miami International Airport reportedly told a bystander his career was over after the fiery Boeing 767 wreck.
item.content:encoded:
After an Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport, killing five people, one of the pilots reportedly told his wife over the phone that his "career was over," according to a new report.

Abraham Altamar told CBS News that he had witnessed the fiery wreck on Sunday while he was working in a nearby building. He did not identify which of the two pilots he spoke with.

Altamar was on FaceTime with his wife when he said the pilot approached him.

"He was, like, shaking and, and a little injured in his forehead and his hand," Altamar said. "I was like, 'Hey, you want me to call 911?' He's like, 'No, we already called them.'"

AMAZON CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS MIAMI AIRPORT RUNWAY AND STRIKES 'MULTIPLE' VEHICLES; 5 DEAD, 5 INJURED

The pilot then called his wife on Altamar's phone to tell her what had happened, CBS reported.

Altamar said the pilot told his wife that he was fine, while instructing her to tell his mother that he was in an accident but survived.

During this conversation, the pilot also reportedly said, "My career is over."

The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office identified the two pilots as Joseph Carroll, 55, and Jaime Felipe Silva Molina, 37.

UPS PLANE ABORTS LANDING IN NEAR MISS AT SAME AIRPORT WHERE NOVEMBER CRASH KILLED 15

A LinkedIn profile for Carroll lists him as a captain for 21 Air, the company operating the plane that crashed over the weekend. A profile for Molina lists him as a first officer at 21 Air.

Federal Aviation Administration records show both men hold airline transport pilot certificates and are qualified to fly Boeing 767 aircraft, the model involved in the Miami crash.

The aircraft was on its third flight of the day when it tried landing at Miami International.

FRONTIER JET STRIKES, KILLS PERSON ON DENVER AIRPORT RUNWAY DURING TAKEOFF AFTER SECURITY BREACH

The jet overshot the runway by at least 1,300 feet beyond the paved surface before crashing into multiple vehicles, including a 2012 white Ford Econoline van with passengers inside, National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said during a Monday press conference.

The aircraft then crashed through the airport perimeter and struck a civilian vehicle, a Toyota Corolla Cross LE.

On Tuesday, Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz released the names of the five people who were killed, all of whom were inside vehicles that were hit by the plane.

They were identified as: Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and 47-year-old Javierkys Reyes Quevedo.

Five others were injured, including the pilots, who were treated and released. The other three people remained hospitalized as of Tuesday, with two of them in critical condition.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office for additional comment.

item.title: Nick Offerman says 'Parks and Rec' character would 'listen to reason' and reconsider his libertarian beliefs
item.description: Actor Nick Offerman claimed on a podcast Sunday that his "Parks and Rec" character Ron Swanson would "listen to reason" and abandon libertarianism eventually.
item.content:encoded:
Former "Parks and Recreation" actor Nick Offerman said Sunday that his famously libertarian-minded character Ron Swanson would eventually "listen to reason" and reconsider his libertarian beliefs.

During an appearance on "Talk Easy with Sam Fragoso," Offerman commented on his 2025 film "Sovereign," in which he played "sovereign citizen" Jerry Kane, who died during a police shootout during a traffic stop in 2010.

Offerman said playing Kane allowed him to sympathize with people like Kane who have been "preyed upon" by "misinformed groups." However, he ultimately dismissed worldviews like Kane's, arguing that libertarianism "can never work."

AMERICA LOST WHAT'S 'LEFT OF ITS INNOCENCE' AFTER TRUMP, 'PARKS AND REC' STAR SAYS

"In order to have a functioning society, that's why libertarianism can never work," Offerman said. "Like on paper, the ideas are great, but it's going to just lead to anarchy because everyone is then open to interpret things, and whoever has the most guns ends up winning. And that's a dumb idea."

"That would be a tough realization for Ron Swanson," Fragoso said.

"I suppose, but I like to think as a Mike Schur character that he would listen to reason eventually," Offerman said.

'COMICS FOR KAMALA' CROONS 'GOD BLESS THE U.S.A.' PARODY: 'PROUD TO BE A KAMALA MAN'

In 2025, Offerman told IndieWire that "Parks and Recreation" creator Mike Schur told him that his character would have "despised" President Donald Trump despite his mistrust of the government.

"Dumb people insist that Ron Swanson would’ve voted for Trump. And I don’t deign to answer myself. I take it to Mike Schur, the main creator of Ron, and he said, ‘Swanson would’ve despised Trump, because Ron loved capitalism. And Trump made the stupidest move you could make as a capitalist, which is to go into public service,’" the actor said.

BILLY BOB THORNTON PUSHES BACK ON CELEBRITY ACTIVISM: ‘I DON'T KNOW ANYTHING ABOUT POLITICS’

In another 2025 interview, Offerman added that he did sympathize with Trump supporters despite their different political views.

"Dealing with Trump supporters in the world is something I try to handle with nuance, because I know many others around the states who are very good people and citizens and would give you the shirt off their back," Offerman said. "They are on the receiving end of an absolute firehose of misinformation, so it's really cognitively dissonant (impossible) to engage in rational discourse."

Bill D'Agostino, the media editor and senior research analyst for the Media Research Center's NewsBusters, told Fox News Digital: "Ron Swanson is a modern-day Archie Bunker: a conservative character whose over-the-top politics endeared him to the people his creators had intended to mock. Swanson is a caricature of exactly the kind of person that his portrayer, Nick Offerman, can’t stand."

D’Agostino added, "Offerman was likely sick of being adored by the people whom he regarded as having missed the joke. He saw two possible solutions: either condemn the character and spend the rest of his life trying to outrun him, or else to cook up a stilted headcanon where Swanson eventually "sees the light" and becomes a limousine liberal like the actor who played him."

D’Agostino concluded, "It doesn’t really matter which of those options Offerman picked. What matters is that in his mind, the only unacceptable course of action was simply to let Ron Swanson continue being Ron Swanson."

item.title: Skillet's John Cooper says woke activists have 'big hearts' but are 'hurting themselves'

item.content:encoded:
Skillet frontman John Cooper believes people labeled "woke" are often motivated by good intentions — but warned their approach can ultimately "hurt society."

"I think it’s really worth mentioning that people that we would call woke, the things that we find really problematic, I think it's worth mentioning that most of those people really have big hearts," Cooper said during a recent appearance on the "Unashamed with the Robertson Family" podcast. "They want justice. They want the world to be better."

"They’re just going about it in a way that they don’t know is wrong, and it’s actually hurting them," he continued. "It’s hurting everybody. It hurts society."

SKILLET’S JOHN COOPER SAYS CHRISTIANS WHO CALL ROCK MUSIC ‘DEMONIC’ ARE ‘GETTING THE GOSPEL WRONG’

He said that inner cities in particular are "getting so much worse," saying, "I look at the things that the politicians that say they want to help the poor, they want to help the marginalized, they want to help people of color, whatever it may be, and all they do is keep hurting them more and more and more."

Cooper said he believes that "the woke probably have good intentions," and pointed to people he knows personally as proof.

"I know these people. Some of them work for me. They’ve worked for me for 15 years. I love them," he said. "And I say to them, ‘I know you’re trying to be a good person, but it’s going to hurt people.’"

The musician ultimately attributed his disagreement with those views to his Christian faith.

"What they’re doing is not true, and it’s not based on the Bible," Cooper said. "It goes against the way God tells us how to live. "I would never say that, because that’s not what art is," he added.

Cooper said he has shared the stage with artists who are atheists and even those who openly oppose Christianity.

"Some of them, I would say, are probably personally not only atheist, they probably personally are a little anti-Christ," he said. "And they would know it. They would say, ‘The truth is, John, I just hate the concept of Jesus.’ And we’re still friends."

item.title: Trump’s pressure campaign has Iran reeling. America can’t hesitate now
item.description: Operation Epic Fury has degraded entire categories of Iran's military, but the United States faces concerns over Russian and Chinese IRGC support.
item.content:encoded:
Iranian officials claim the regime is "confident" and are considering escalation against the United States. Iran may indeed lash out, but it would be coming from a place of desperation, not strength. On Saturday, Sept. 5, U.S. Central Command struck three Iranian tankers. "Let ‌the message to the IRGC be clear: ‌If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — ⁠taking out⁠ three of yours," said Admiral Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command. Three days later, U.S. Central Command said it destroyed five more tankers, after the IRGC "targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days."

President Donald Trump has chosen to crush the Iranian regime economically, but U.S. military strikes (that are hitting their intended targets at an astoundingly near-perfect success rate) continue to play a major role. The combination of the blockade, sanctions and periodic punishing strikes has crippled the Iranian regime’s ability to impose much harm to the United States or its allies. The current course is not a permanent solution to the Iranian regime problem, but the United States is winning, and the public narrative should reflect that.

The U.S. strikes were in response to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) failed attempts to hit U.S. Navy ships. U.S. officials told reporters last week that half of the 25 ballistic missiles Iran fired toward Jordan failed to so much as enter Jordanian airspace.

TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS

What should we make of this? The regime has always been bad at targeting, but all of its challenges have been exacerbated by the U.S. and Israeli campaigns, and whatever help it continues to receive from the Russians or Chinese does appear to be limited in its effectiveness. This shouldn’t get these other Iranian backers off the hook for supporting our enemies in a hot war, but it does give credence to the Trump administration’s contention that so far, the help the Iranian regime is receiving hasn’t had a meaningful impact in the IRGC’s favor.

We don't know much more about what the United States is doing to prevent other nations from assisting Iran, but Russian and Chinese support for the Iranian regime continues to be my No. 1 concern about the possible duration and expansion of the war and something to track closely.

BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY

And as for diplomacy? Trump has concluded correctly that those in power in Tehran are not ready to make a deal. "I couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement. I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?" Trump wrote on social media.

This is good news, as the short-lived so-called Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) permitted the Iranians to sell oil and gave the regime temporary economic reprieve even though the IRGC never intended to stop trying to toll the Strait of Hormuz or shooting at commercial shipping.

TRUMP REVIVES IRAN REGIME CHANGE SPECULATION WITH CRYPTIC CALL FOR PEOPLE TO 'RISE UP'

Just a few weeks ago, critics of Trump and his decision to launch Operation Epic Fury, were insisting that Trump needed to simply leave the Middle East and accept that he led the United States to failure against the Islamic Republic. The popular narrative is that the regime is now "more hardlined" and "more determined" to get a nuclear weapon and now has significant leverage over the United States through its terrorist behavior against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The critics get it wrong and are recycling some of the erroneous assumptions used to prop up President Barack Obama’s "Iran deal." There are no moderates within the Islamic Republic of Iran. The regime has been in dogged pursuit of a nuclear weapon for years, and it was only thwarted through sanctions and now, finally, Trump’s decision to engage militarily. It is a myth that the regime was so formidable that the only course was to accept that the Iranians will have a latent nuclear program, and it is best to simply accept it and try to buy off or appease the regime.

IRAN IS NOT A NORMAL NATION YOU CAN MAKE DEALS WITH; IT’S A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT

U.S. military operations have demonstrated military competency and credibility and have degraded or eliminated entire categories of Iran’s military, significant regime leadership and key industries the regime used to support its military. Now the United States is seeking to cut off the regime’s resources through a very effective naval blockade, sanctions and selective secondary sanctions.

But the use of military strikes also continues in bursts. Trump said Tuesday, Sept. 8, that he is prepared to authorize additional strikes against Iran "any time we want." According to a Wall Street Journal report, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has extended the deployment of approximately 50,000 U.S. troops and 19 warships in the Middle East.

TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME
